topic: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
parentTitle: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
title: Paediatric A-E assessment and physiological differences in deterioration
blurb: Use a quick look, then a structured ABCDE assessment adapted for children, and recognise why children deteriorate differently from adults.
question: An 18-month-old is carried into the children's assessment unit. Before touching him, what should the nurse look for, and how should the ABCDE assessment be adapted for a toddler?

teach.body: Cardiac arrest in children is most often SECONDARY to progressive respiratory or circulatory failure (or a neurological emergency), not a primary heart problem. Children compensate well, then decompensate suddenly. Plain English: catch the breathing or circulation problem early and treat it, and you prevent the arrest.

teach.h: Quick look before you touch: BBB

letters.word: Behaviour: floppy, hard to rouse, inconsolable, abnormal interaction
Breathing: fast, grunting, flaring, recession, noises
Body colour: cyanosed, mottled, pale or grey

teach.caption: RCUK 2025: use a quick-look tool such as BBB or the Paediatric Assessment Triangle, then a full ABCDE. Check palms, soles and mucous membranes in darker skin.

head: Assess
Child-specific points
rows: Stridor or snoring = partial obstruction; let a conscious child sit as they choose
Recession, grunting, nasal flaring, tracheal tug, head bobbing; cry strength
CRT, skin colour and temperature, urine output, conscious level
Check blood glucose; seizures are an emergency
Rashes, injuries, signs of abuse or neglect; AMPLE history

teach.h: Respiratory failure: from compensation to arrest

steps.label: Decompensated
steps.sub: Slow irregular breathing, less effort, silent chest

teach.caption: Less recession in a child who is getting worse can mean exhaustion, not improvement.

teach.body: Open the airway with head tilt and chin lift (or jaw thrust). In infants keep the head in a NEUTRAL position; older children need more head tilt. Do not force a conscious child with airway noise to lie down: let them adopt the position they find most comfortable, often on a parent's lap.

items: Sami is carried in by his mother. Quick look: floppy, grunting with nasal flaring, mottled skin.
Nurse Lin calls for help immediately and starts ABCDE with Sami on his mother's lap.
A: patent, no stridor. B: RR 58, recession, SpO2 89% in air: oxygen. C: HR 175, CRT 4 s. D: responds to voice; glucose checked. E: temperature 39.4°C, no rash.
She records on the 1-4 years PEWS chart, escalates, reassesses after each intervention and keeps his mother informed.

teach.text: Do not be reassured when a struggling child's breathing slows or recession lessens without other improvement: this can be exhaustion. And do not skip D's blood glucose check in a drowsy child.

items.label: HR with poor perfusion despite ventilation: compressions

items: Quick look first (BBB or Paediatric Assessment Triangle), then ABCDE.
Neutral head in infants; let a conscious child choose their position.
Work of breathing: recession, grunting, flaring, tracheal tug, head bobbing.
Circulation: HR, CRT, skin, urine output, conscious level; hypotension is late.
Check glucose in D; fully expose in E and look for rashes and signs of abuse.

summary: You can now perform a quick look and a child-adapted ABCDE assessment, recognise compensation and the signs of decompensation, position a child's airway correctly, and explain why children deteriorate differently from adults.

A.q: Sami, 18 months, is carried into the assessment unit by his mother. Before touching him, what should the nurse assess first?
options: Behaviour, breathing and colour by looking
Blood pressure with a correctly sized cuff
Capillary refill time over the sternum
A.why: RCUK 2025 advises a quick-look tool (BBB or the Paediatric Assessment Triangle) to recognise a critically ill child before a hands-on ABCDE.

whyNot.1: BP is part of C later; it also upsets a toddler before the quick look.
whyNot.3: CRT is a hands-on C assessment that comes after the quick look.

A.q: Freddie, 4 months, is found unresponsive in his cot and breathing noisily. The nurse calls for help. How should she position his head to open the airway?
A.why: In infants the head is kept in a neutral position with chin lift; older children need more head tilt.

whyNot.0: Over-extension can obstruct an infant's airway.
whyNot.2: Turning the head does not open the airway.

A.q: What usually causes cardiac arrest in children?
options: Congenital heart disease in most cases
A.why: RCUK 2025: paediatric arrest is most often secondary to progressive respiratory or circulatory failure, or neurological emergencies.

whyNot.0: Primary cardiac causes are uncommon in children.
whyNot.2: Congenital heart disease causes some arrests but not most.
whyNot.3: Electrolyte problems can contribute but are not the usual cause.

B.q: Ellie, 3 months, has bronchiolitis. The nurse hears a short noise at the end of each breath out and sees her nostrils widen with each breath. What do these signs indicate?
options: A normal pattern of breathing in infancy
Grunting and flaring: more work of breathing
B.why: Expiratory grunting and nasal flaring are signs of increased work of breathing (RCUK 2025); grunting can indicate tiring.

whyNot.0: Grunting and flaring are not normal.
whyNot.1: Upper airway obstruction causes snoring or stridor, usually on inspiration.
whyNot.3: Wheeze is a prolonged musical sound, not a short grunt at the end of expiration.

B.q: Daniel, 7, has acute asthma. An hour ago he had marked recession and RR 40. Now his recession is less obvious, RR is 18, he is drowsy and his chest sounds quiet. What does this indicate?
options: He is responding well to treatment
Exhaustion with a silent chest: life-threatening
He is falling asleep after a tiring night
His wheeze has resolved so oxygen can stop
B.why: Falling RR with drowsiness and a quiet chest is decompensation; silent chest is a life-threatening feature (SIGN 244, RCUK Table 2).

whyNot.0: Improvement would come with better air entry and alertness, not drowsiness.
whyNot.2: Drowsiness here reflects hypoxia or hypercapnia, not normal sleep.
whyNot.3: A silent chest means little air is moving; oxygen and urgent escalation are needed.

B.q: Leah, 2, has had diarrhoea and vomiting for 2 days and now responds only to voice. Airway and breathing are satisfactory. During D, which check must the nurse not miss?
B.why: RCUK 2025 includes checking blood glucose in the D assessment; hypoglycaemia can cause reduced consciousness and is treatable.

whyNot.0: Head circumference is a growth measure, not part of D in an acute assessment.
whyNot.1: Peak flow is for asthma in older children and is not part of D.
whyNot.2: Urine testing may help later but is not the critical D check.

C.q: During the E part of an ABCDE assessment of Kai, a 5-month-old with suspected sepsis, what should the nurse do?
options: Undress him, check temperature, look for rashes
Keep him clothed to prevent any heat loss
Examine the areas his parents point out
Expose him and leave him uncovered to cool down
C.why: E includes temperature and full exposure to look for rashes, injuries and signs of abuse, while preventing heat loss by recovering him afterwards.

whyNot.1: A non-blanching rash or injury could be missed if he stays clothed.
whyNot.2: Full exposure is needed; important signs may not be noticed by parents.
whyNot.3: He should be covered again after examination to prevent heat loss.

C.q: Oscar, 3, has croup with stridor at rest. He is sitting upright on his father's lap and is distressed when moved. What should the nurse do?
options: Lie him flat to assess his chest properly
Examine his throat with a tongue depressor
Let him stay upright on his father's lap
Separate him from his father for assessment
C.why: RCUK 2025: allow a conscious child to adopt the most comfortable position; keeping him calm and upright avoids worsening obstruction. Do not examine the throat.

whyNot.0: Forcing him to lie down can worsen obstruction and distress.
whyNot.1: Examining the throat can precipitate complete obstruction.
whyNot.3: Separation increases distress and oxygen demand.

C.q: Mia, 6, has suspected sepsis. HR 150, CRT 4 seconds, cool hands and feet, BP 102/64. The nurse gives oxygen and calls for help. Which statement about her circulation is correct?
options: Her circulation is adequate as BP is normal
She has compensated shock despite a normal BP
Her signs reflect fever, not poor perfusion
Her CRT becomes relevant once BP falls
C.why: Tachycardia, prolonged CRT and cool peripheries are signs of poor perfusion; BP is maintained until late in children, so this is compensated shock.

whyNot.0: Normal BP does not exclude shock in children.
whyNot.2: Prolonged CRT and cool peripheries indicate poor perfusion and must not be attributed to fever.
whyNot.3: CRT is an early sign; waiting for hypotension delays treatment.

reteach.title: Look before you touch
reteach.question: What can you learn about a sick child in the first 10 seconds without touching them?

blocks.body: How does the child behave: alert and interested, or floppy and not interacting? How do they breathe: fast, noisy, working hard? What colour are they: pink, pale, mottled, blue? If any looks wrong, call for help and move straight into ABCDE, treating problems as you find them.

blocks.text: Less effort plus a worse child = tiring. Do not mistake it for recovery.

explain.body: Look, listen, feel. Stridor or snoring means partial obstruction. Neutral head in infants, more tilt in older children. Let a conscious child choose their position.

test.q: Which sound suggests partial upper airway obstruction in a child?
test.why: RCUK 2025: consider stridor or snoring to be a sign of partial airway obstruction.

whyNot.0: Crackles suggest fluid or infection in the lower airways.
whyNot.2: A silent chest is a life-threatening sign of minimal air entry, not upper airway noise.

explain.body: Work of breathing (RR, recession, grunting, flaring, tracheal tug, head bobbing, position), effectiveness (chest expansion, cry, air entry, colour, SpO2) and effects (HR, conscious level).

test.q: Which finding is a sign of increased work of breathing in an infant?
test.why: Head bobbing is a sign of respiratory distress listed on the national PEWS chart.

whyNot.2: A strong cry suggests effective breathing.
whyNot.3: A short CRT reflects good perfusion.

explain.body: HR, pulse volume, BP, and perfusion: CRT, skin colour and temperature, urine output, conscious level. BP falls late; bradycardia is pre-arrest.

test.q: Which is a late sign of circulatory failure in a child?
test.why: Hypotension appears when compensation fails (RCUK Table 2).

whyNot.0: Tachycardia is an early compensatory sign.
whyNot.1: Cool peripheries are an early sign of vasoconstriction.
whyNot.3: Prolonged CRT is an early sign of poor perfusion.

explain.body: AVPU or paediatric GCS, pupils, posture, blood glucose. Then temperature and full exposure for rashes, injuries and signs of abuse or neglect; cover again to keep warm. Take an AMPLE history.

test.q: In a drowsy child, which D check is essential because the cause is quickly treatable?
test.why: RCUK 2025 includes blood glucose in D; hypoglycaemia is quickly treatable with 10% glucose.

whyNot.1: Blood pressure is assessed in C.
whyNot.2: Respiratory rate is assessed in B.
whyNot.3: Peak flow is an asthma measure in older children, not part of D.
